warmup: Think first: your instrument learner flew good holds last week. Today she arrives late from work, flies the first approach well, then falls apart when ATC changes her clearance. In the debrief she says the controller 'talked way too fast' and answers 'yes' when you ask if she understands what happened. What do you see in her behavior, and what in your own words and questions might be part of the problem?

key_terms.def: What the study of human behavior tries to explain: how and why humans function the way they do. Behavior is a product of innate human nature and of individual experience and environment [[25:34|AIH 2-1]].
A need or desire that causes a person to act. It can be positive or negative, tangible or intangible, subtle or obvious [[25:212|AIH G-4]].
Maslow's listing of needs from the most basic to the most fulfilling: physiological, security, belonging, esteem, cognitive and aesthetic, and self-actualization [[25:211|AIH G-3]].
The learner's basic needs have to be satisfied before he or she is ready or capable of learning; the instructor can do little to motivate a learner whose needs are not met [[25:62|AIH 3-11]].
Subconscious ego-protecting reactions to unpleasant situations [[25:210|AIH G-2]]. They often appear unconsciously and tend to distort, transform or falsify reality [[25:42|AIH 2-9]].

The AIH says that in some ways an aviation instructor serves as a practical psychologist, a responsibility met by being familiar and conversant in the fundamentals of instructing and by careful analysis of and continuing interest in learners [[25:160|AIH 8-2]].
A response to anxiety or stress that is completely absent or inadequate, random or illogical, or more than the situation calls for [[25:48|AIH 2-15]].
In communication, the sender, speaker, transmitter or instructor who composes and transmits a message made up of symbols meaningful to listeners and readers [[25:214|AIH G-6]].

Simple oral and visual codes such as words, gestures and facial expressions, formed into sentences, paragraphs, lectures or chapters that mean something to the receiver [[25:214|AIH G-6]]. The text adds tactile codes [[25:95|AIH 4-2]].
The listener, reader or learner who takes in a message, processes it, reacts with understanding and changes behavior in accordance with the message [[25:213|AIH G-5]].
Words that are general rather than specific. Aircraft is an abstraction; airplane is less abstract; jet is more specific; jet airliner is more specific still [[25:209|AIH G-1]].

A message disrupted, truncated or added to somewhere in the communication sequence, while both people may believe it arrived intact [[25:99|AIH 4-6]]. The glossary also uses the word for barriers caused by factors outside the instructor's control [[25:212|AIH G-4]].

chunks.title: From PTS words to today's AIH words

body.p: The PTS asks you to describe the elements of human behavior and effective communication as they apply to the teaching and learning process, and it lists FAA-H-8083-9 as the reference [[FAA-S-8081-9E:23|PTS I.B]]. It also tells users to reference the current edition of each document [[FAA-S-8081-9E:8|PTS References NOTE]]. In the current Aviation Instructor's Handbook, FAA-H-8083-9B, the two halves are Chapter 2, Human Behavior, and Chapter 4, Effective Communication [[25:34|AIH 2-1]] [[25:94|AIH 4-1]]. The CFI lesson FI.I.A teaches the same two chapters from the CFI ACS and goes deeper on motivation, emotional reactions, fatigue and the adult learner. This lesson follows the seven PTS items one by one and uses instrument training examples.

body.p: **Why the two halves are one Task.** The AIH lists people skills first among four essential teaching skills, says effective communication underlies people skills, and reminds instructors that technical knowledge is useless if it is not communicated effectively [[25:104|AIH 5-1]] [[25:105|AIH 5-2]]. Its Teaching Process chapter describes taking these concepts about human behavior, how people learn and effective communication into the classroom and turning them into practical teaching methods [[25:104|AIH 5-1]].

callout.text: Application: say the PTS phrase first, then answer in the current AIH words. The PTS says student; the AIH says learner. Evaluators are told to test application and correlation and to use scenario-based questions when possible [[FAA-S-8081-9E:14|PTS Evaluator Responsibility]], so have one instrument learner example ready for each of the seven items.

check.q: The examiner asks you to describe 'control of human behavior.' Where in the current AIH do you look?
check.a: There is no heading by that name in FAA-H-8083-9B. Answer from what drives behavior (needs, experience, life course) [[25:34|AIH 2-1]], motivation [[25:35|AIH 2-2]], the two systems that compete for control of behavior [[25:41|AIH 2-8]], and how perception and threat shape behavior [[25:59|AIH 3-8]].

chunks.title: Control of human behavior I: what drives it

body.p: **Control of human behavior.** The current AIH has no section with this title. Instead it explains what drives behavior, which is what you need to know in order to influence it. Human behavior is a product both of innate human nature and of individual experience and environment [[25:34|AIH 2-1]]. The AIH defines it three ways: as the product of factors that cause people to act in predictable ways, as the result of attempts to satisfy needs, and through the typical life course, in which people move from dependency to self-direction [[25:34|AIH 2-1]]. FI.I.A works through each definition. For this Task the point is that behavior has causes you can observe: by watching behavior you learn about the learner's needs and about yourself as an instructor [[25:34|AIH 2-1]].

**The behaviorist view of control.** Behaviorism explains behavior entirely by observable, measurable responses to stimuli, so behavior can be predicted from past rewards and punishments, the 'carrot and stick' [[25:54|AIH 3-3]]. In modern education it stresses having a behavior positively reinforced by someone other than the learner who shapes or controls what is learned; in aviation training, the instructor provides that reinforcement [[25:54|AIH 3-3]]. The AIH also gives the limit: learning is more complex than a response to stimuli, and humans are always actively interacting with their environment [[25:54|AIH 3-3]]. The law of effect points the same way: behaviors that lead to satisfying outcomes are likely to be repeated, so create situations that promote success [[25:63|AIH 3-12]].

**Behavior follows perception.** A learner's behavior is directly influenced by the way the learner perceives [[25:59|AIH 3-8]]. Fear narrows the perceptual field: a threatened learner limits attention to the threatening object or condition. In the AIH example, Beverly fixes on the altimeter during her first steep turns and disregards outside references [[25:59|AIH 3-8]]. The IFH describes the same pattern under the hood: while a pilot stares at one instrument, tension may be unconsciously exerted on the controls and cause an unnoticed heading change, and uncertainty about instrument interpretation or about control may cause a fixation [[23:146|IFH 6-13]].

Learning is a psychological process, not necessarily a logical one. Threats of unsatisfactory reports or reprisals may seem logical but are not effective psychologically. As long as the learner feels able to cope, each new experience is viewed as a challenge rather than a threat [[25:59|AIH 3-8]].

callout.text: Application: when a learner under the hood fixates and tenses up, lower the threat before you add words. Take the controls with a positive exchange if needed, let the learner settle, then rebuild the cross-check one instrument at a time. A frightened learner's attention is limited to the threat [[25:59|AIH 3-8]].

check.q: Your learner fixates on the altimeter during her first steep turns under the hood. Why will a stern 'you'll fail the stage check like this' make it worse?
check.a: Threat narrows the perceptual field onto the threatening thing, and threats of unsatisfactory reports are not effective psychologically [[25:59|AIH 3-8]]. Fixation under the hood often comes from uncertainty about interpretation or control [[23:146|IFH 6-13]], so reduce the threat and rebuild the skill.

chunks.title: Control of human behavior II: steering with motivation and goals

body.p: Motivation is the reason one acts or behaves a certain way, and the AIH calls it probably the dominant force that governs the learner's progress and ability to understand [[25:35|AIH 2-2]]. Positive motivation, the promise or achievement of rewards, promotes learning better than negative motivation, which may engender fear [[25:35|AIH 2-2]]. Avoid negative motivation with all but the most overconfident and impulsive learners, and expect motivation to rise and fall with outside influences or inadequate instruction [[25:37|AIH 2-4]].

**Two systems compete for control.** Kahneman describes System 1, fast, automatic and emotional, and System 2, slow, logical and effortful. The two constantly compete for control of the behaviors that affect decision-making, and once the immediate problem is solved, System 1 takes over again [[25:41|AIH 2-8]]. Knowing this helps you spot learner pitfalls: assuming a complex problem is a simple one, or reusing a recent solution on a task that only looks similar [[25:42|AIH 2-9]].

**Goals steer effort.** Difficult but possible goals usually provide a challenge and promote learning. In a flight lesson, reasonable goals go in the lesson objectives and the desired proficiency goes in completion standards [[25:43|AIH 2-10]]. Impossible or unreasonable goals discourage the learner, diminish effort and retard learning, as in Figure 2-6 [[25:44|AIH 2-11]], and motivation declines when the learner believes the instructor's demands are unreasonable [[25:43|AIH 2-10]].

**Your own conduct steers behavior.** Learners want to please their instructor, so if the same thing is acceptable one day and unacceptable the next, they become confused [[25:162|AIH 8-4]]. The successful instructor avoids contradictory directions, reacting differently to similar errors at different times, demanding unreasonable performance or progress, and criticizing unfairly [[25:167|AIH 8-9]].
The AIH sums up what keeps learners working hard [[25:38|AIH 2-5]]:

bullets: Ask new learners about their aviation training goals [[25:38|AIH 2-5]].
Occasionally remind learners of their own stated goals [[25:38|AIH 2-5]].
Assure learners that plateaus are normal and that improvement will resume with continued effort [[25:38|AIH 2-5]].

callout.text: Application: write the completion standard into the lesson plan, brief it before engine start and grade to it afterward. The goal is then reasonable and stated in advance [[25:43|AIH 2-10]], and your reaction is the same on every flight [[25:162|AIH 8-4]].

check.q: Figure 2-6 shows an instructor saying 'I said 3,000 feet... not 2,990!' What does the AIH say that kind of demand does to the learner?
check.a: Impossible or unreasonable goals discourage the learner, diminish effort and retard learning [[25:44|AIH 2-11]]. Set difficult but possible goals, with completion standards, in the lesson objectives [[25:43|AIH 2-10]].

body.p: **Human needs** are things all humans require for normal growth and development [[25:38|AIH 2-5]]. Henry Murray (1938) described primary needs, based on biology such as the need for food, and secondary needs, generally psychological such as the need for independence [[25:38|AIH 2-5]]. Abraham Maslow noticed that some needs take precedence over others, such as thirst before hunger, and in 1954 published his hierarchy: needs are satisfied in order of importance, and once one is satisfied, people work on the next [[25:38|AIH 2-5]].

body.p: The AIH glossary lists the levels as physiological, security, belonging, esteem, cognitive and aesthetic, and self-actualization [[25:211|AIH G-3]], while Figure 2-3 shows five. The aim is a healthy learning environment: learners who can satisfy their needs have fewer frustrations and can give more attention to their studies [[25:40|AIH 2-7]].

check.q: Which level did Maslow add later, and what flight training moment does the AIH use to show it?
check.a: Cognitive and aesthetic needs. The need to know and understand is rewarded with a rush of dopamine, the 'eureka!' moment, such as completing the first solo [[25:40|AIH 2-7]].

chunks.title: Human needs in the lesson: readiness and the pre-assessment

body.p: The AIH presents Maslow and then qualifies him. Later studies showed people can reach higher levels of motivation without lower needs met; a 2011 study found the hierarchy was not universal and the order in which needs were met had little impact; and the five-need hierarchy has little to no empirical data behind it [[25:38|AIH 2-5]].

What the studies did show is that unmet needs pull attention away from the task. A hungry learner's focus of perception is on satisfying the need, not on the instructor; an anxious learner attempting a first full stall focuses on the 'flee' response, not the skill [[25:38|AIH 2-5]]. Needs do not have to be met 100 percent, and the order they are met in has little to no effect on learning. What matters is that you verify most needs are met (the law of readiness) and then focus the learner's senses on the lesson [[25:39|AIH 2-6]].

**Law of readiness.** The learner's basic needs have to be satisfied before he or she is ready or capable of learning, and the instructor can do little to motivate a learner whose needs are not met [[25:62|AIH 3-11]]. To satisfy it, conduct a thorough **pre-assessment** before the lesson to verify the learner is physically and mentally ready to learn [[25:39|AIH 2-6]].

Application: the AIH gives IMSAFE as a checklist pilots may use to assess their own fitness before flight: Illness, Medication, Stress, Alcohol, Fatigue and Emotion. Its Stress item asks about pressure from the job and money, health or family problems [[25:12|AIH 1-8]]. Walking a learner through the same six items gives the pre-assessment a structure. Also watch for physiological obstacles such as unfamiliar noise, vibration, G-forces and stomach discomfort. Do not ignore them or ridicule a learner who is affected; a sick learner is preoccupied and may not have the capacity to learn [[25:163|AIH 8-5]].

callout.text: Application: make the pre-assessment a two-minute chat at the start of every instrument lesson: 'When did you last eat? How did you sleep? Anything on your mind today?' If the answers say the learner is not ready, change the plan to a shorter flight, a training device session or a ground lesson.

check.q: Your learner says, 'I skipped lunch and slept four hours, but let's fly the approaches anyway.' Does Maslow's order decide whether you go?
check.a: No. The AIH says the order has little effect; what matters is whether most needs are met so you can focus the learner's perception on the lesson [[25:39|AIH 2-6]]. Hunger pulls attention to the need [[25:38|AIH 2-5]], so deal with it or change the lesson.

chunks.title: Defense mechanisms: what they are and the eight common ones

body.p: **Defense mechanisms** can be biological or psychological [[25:42|AIH 2-9]]. The biological one is the 'fight or flight' response, with adrenaline, a rapid heart rate and higher blood pressure. When an anxious learner meets impending and full stalls, the AIH says to take the procedure apart, demonstrate each stage and let the learner practice the stages in realistic scenarios until confidence grows [[25:42|AIH 2-9]].

The psychological **ego defense mechanism**, introduced by Freud in 1894, is an unconscious mental process that protects a person from anxiety or unpleasant emotions, or gives refuge from a situation the person cannot yet cope with. It softens feelings of failure, alleviates guilt, helps the person cope with reality and protects self-image [[25:42|AIH 2-9]]. When the mind cannot solve a problem or escape it, defense mechanisms are triggered. They share two properties: they often appear unconsciously, and they tend to distort, transform or falsify reality. Repression and denial are the two primary ones [[25:42|AIH 2-9]].

AIH meaning
Instrument training example (application)
rows: Repression

Uncomfortable thoughts are pushed into inaccessible areas of the unconscious and may reappear in dreams or slips of the tongue. Example: a repressed fear of flying that inhibits learning to fly [[25:42|AIH 2-9]]
A learner who once had a frightening inadvertent IMC encounter recalls little of it, and his progress slows as soon as cloud flying begins
Denial
Refusing to accept an external reality because it is too threatening. In minimization, the person accepts what happened, but in a diluted form [[25:42|AIH 2-9]]
Denial: 'I never went below the MDA,' though the track log shows he did. Minimization: 'I was a bit low, but nothing happened'
Compensation
Counterbalancing a perceived weakness by emphasizing strength in another area [[25:43|AIH 2-10]]
Weak on holding, a learner turns every debrief to his excellent crosswind landings
Projection
Placing one's own unacceptable impulses, or the blame for one's own shortcomings, on someone else: 'I failed because I had a poor examiner' [[25:43|AIH 2-10]]
'The controller rushed the clearance; that is why I flew the wrong entry'
Rationalization
A subconscious technique for justifying actions that would otherwise be unacceptable, with plausible excuses the person sincerely believes [[25:43|AIH 2-10]]
'Work was too busy to study the plates,' while the approach briefing practice you assigned went undone
Reaction formation
Faking a belief opposite to the true one, because the true belief causes anxiety [[25:44|AIH 2-11]]
A learner anxious about her first flight in actual IMC loudly insists she cannot wait to get into the clouds
Fantasy

Daydreaming about how things should be instead of doing anything about how they are. The AIH's transitioning pilot dreams of the airline job instead of mastering the complex airplane [[25:44|AIH 2-11]]
A learner talks about flying night freight in IMC but never prepares for the next approach lesson
Displacement
An unconscious shift of emotion from its real object to a more acceptable, less threatening substitute [[25:44|AIH 2-11]]
Angry at the check instructor over a grade, he is curt with the scheduler instead

check.q: Why does the AIH call defense mechanisms a poor fix, even though most of them are normal?
check.a: They involve some self-deception and distortion of reality, so they alleviate the symptoms, not the causes, and do not solve problems [[25:44|AIH 2-11]].

chunks.title: When defenses take over: signs and what you do

body.p: Most defense mechanisms fall within normal behavior and serve a useful purpose, but they relieve symptoms, not causes [[25:44|AIH 2-11]]. Because they work on an unconscious level, they are not subject to normal conscious checks and balances; once a person realizes he is consciously relying on one, it stops being an unconscious adjustment and becomes an ineffective way of satisfying a need [[25:44|AIH 2-11]].

**Warning signs.** Excessive reliance on defense mechanisms is hard for an instructor to identify, but a personal crisis or other stressful event is usually the cause: a death in the family, a divorce or even a failing grade on an important test [[25:44|AIH 2-11]]. Look for a change in personality, angry outbursts, depression or a general lack of interest; drug or alcohol abuse may also become apparent. Less obvious signs are social withdrawal, preoccupation with certain ideas and an inability to concentrate [[25:44|AIH 2-11]].
**What the AIH says you do** [[25:45|AIH 2-12]]:

bullets: Be familiar with the typical defense mechanisms and have some knowledge of related behavior problems [[25:45|AIH 2-12]].
Use common sense and discuss the problem with the learner. The main objective is to restore motivation and self-confidence [[25:45|AIH 2-12]].
Remember that the human psyche is fragile and can be damaged by inept measures [[25:45|AIH 2-12]].
In severe cases involving possible deep psychological problems, recommend that the learner use the services of a professional counselor [[25:45|AIH 2-12]].

body.p: **Instructors have defenses too.** The AIH notes that continued use of outmoded instructional procedures, or preparing learners to obsolete certification requirements, usually involves rationalization [[25:165|AIH 8-7]]. Application: teaching an instrument learner a procedure that has since changed is a ready example, so keep your own references current.

callout.text: Application: in the debrief, do not hand the learner a label ('that is projection'). Describe what happened, in private and without judgment, as the AIH advises for negative feedback [[25:96|AIH 4-3]]. The mechanism is unconscious and not subject to normal conscious checks [[25:44|AIH 2-11]], so a calm talk about the facts serves the goal of restoring motivation and self-confidence [[25:45|AIH 2-12]] better than an argument.

check.q: Since his divorce your learner's interest has dropped, he can't concentrate, and he blames ATC for every mistake. What do you do?
check.a: A personal crisis like a divorce can trigger harmful defensive reactions, and an inability to concentrate is one of the signs [[25:44|AIH 2-11]]. Discuss it with him using common sense, aiming to restore motivation and self-confidence; if deep psychological problems seem possible, recommend a professional counselor [[25:45|AIH 2-12]].

chunks.title: The flight instructor as a practical psychologist

body.p: **The flight instructor as a practical psychologist.** The AIH uses the phrase directly: 'In some ways, an aviation instructor serves as a practical psychologist.' You meet that responsibility by becoming familiar and conversant in the fundamentals of instructing and through a careful analysis of, and continuing interest in, your learners [[25:160|AIH 8-2]]. You do not need to be a certified psychologist, but it helps to learn to analyze learner behavior before and during each flight lesson, so you can develop and use appropriate techniques for the instruction still to come [[25:45|AIH 2-12]].

**Analyze, then tailor.** No two learners are alike. Analyze each learner's personality, thinking and ability, talk with the learner at some length about background, interests, temperament and way of thinking, and be ready to change your methods as the learner advances. An incorrect analysis means the instruction may not produce the desired results [[25:159|AIH 8-1]].

'She is just a slow learner'
She may understand the situation but lack self-confidence; direct instruction toward building self-confidence rather than drill on fundamentals [[25:159|AIH 8-1]]

Use tact, keen perception and delicate handling; too much help and encouragement can create a feeling of incompetence [[25:159|AIH 8-1]]

'Fly the whole maneuver until it clicks'
Assign more easily attained goals, and split a complex task into elements to practice one at a time [[25:160|AIH 8-2]]

'Leave him alone, he is fine'

He may think correcting errors is unimportant and become overconfident; raise the standard each lesson, but never invent deficiencies, since unfair criticism destroys confidence in you [[25:160|AIH 8-2]]

body.p: **Read the emotions too.** Anxiety is probably the most significant psychological factor affecting flight instruction, and responses range from hesitancy to act to the impulse to do something even if it is wrong [[25:45|AIH 2-12]]. Treat fears as a normal reaction, and introduce anxiety-causing maneuvers with care so learners know what to expect and what their reaction should be [[25:45|AIH 2-12]]. The AIH's instrument example: a learner anticipating drastic changes in routing becomes anxious and finds it very hard to listen to and process the new route [[25:101|AIH 4-8]]. FI.I.A covers impatience, worry and lack of interest in depth.

How you carry yourself is part of the job. The AIH asks for a calm, thoughtful and disciplined demeanor, without erratic movements, distracting speech habits or capricious changes in mood [[25:167|AIH 8-9]]. It also warns that new instructors tend to adopt their own instructors' methods, which were not necessarily the best, so stay open-minded [[25:160|AIH 8-2]].

check.q: Your quiet learner explains the missed approach perfectly in the debrief but is late to start it in the airplane. What is the AIH's read, and your plan?
check.a: A quiet, reserved learner may fail to act at the proper time from lack of self-confidence even though the situation is understood. Direct the instruction toward building self-confidence rather than more drill on fundamentals [[25:159|AIH 8-1]].

chunks.title: Stress reactions and the seriously abnormal learner

body.p: **Normal reactions to stress.** When a threat is recognized or imagined, the body prepares to meet it or retreat from it, the fight or flight syndrome. Normal individuals respond rapidly and exactly within the limits of their experience and training, think rationally, act rapidly and are extremely sensitive to all aspects of their surroundings. Many responses are automatic, which highlights the need for proper training in emergency operations before an actual emergency [[25:48|AIH 2-15]].

**Abnormal reactions to stress.** In some people the response is completely absent or inadequate, random or illogical, or more than the situation calls for [[25:48|AIH 2-15]]. During flight instruction you are normally the only one who sees the learner under pressure, so you are the one who can tell safe from unsafe piloting actions and may detect potential psychological problems. None of these signs is an absolute indication, but any of them under stress is reason for careful evaluation [[25:48|AIH 2-15]]:

bullets: Inappropriate reactions: extreme over-cooperation, painstaking self-control, inappropriate laughter or singing, very rapid changes in emotion [[25:48|AIH 2-15]].
Marked changes in mood on different lessons, such as excellent morale followed by deep depression [[25:48|AIH 2-15]].
Severe anger directed toward the flight instructor, service personnel and others [[25:48|AIH 2-15]].

body.p: **Seriously abnormal learners.** If you believe a learner may have a serious psychological abnormality, you have a responsibility to refrain from instructing that learner, and a personal responsibility to make sure the person does not continue flight training or become certificated [[25:49|AIH 2-16]]. Arrange an evaluation flight with another instructor who is not acquainted with the learner; afterward the two of you confer on whether further investigation or action is justified. Your primary legal responsibility is the decision to endorse solo or recommend the practical test, and if the concern stands after consulting the unbiased instructor, withhold those endorsements and recommendations [[25:49|AIH 2-16]].

**Check yourself too.** In difficult situations, examine your own responses to the learner as well as the learner's responses [[25:48|AIH 2-15]]. Instructors meeting a new avionics suite face the stress of change too, and your own actions and care during training can frame how a learner responds well into the future [[25:49|AIH 2-16]]. A risk assessment tool built into the training program can diminish stress and strengthen a learner's confidence and decision-making [[25:50|AIH 2-17]].

callout.text: Application: you observe and act; you do not diagnose. Write down what you saw in plain behavioral terms (what, when, under what stress) so that you and the unbiased instructor can confer on facts [[25:49|AIH 2-16]].

check.q: Your learner is fine on the ground, but on every approach lesson he laughs loudly and sings when you fail an instrument. What do you do?
check.a: Inappropriate laughter or singing under stress is one of the AIH's signs of an abnormal reaction. It is not an absolute indication, but it calls for careful evaluation [[25:48|AIH 2-15]]. If you come to believe there is a serious problem, arrange an evaluation flight with an instructor who does not know him and confer afterward [[25:49|AIH 2-16]].

chunks.title: Basic elements of communication: source, symbols, receiver

body.p: **Basic elements of communication.** Communication takes place when one person transmits ideas or feelings to another person or group, and its effectiveness is measured by the similarity between the idea transmitted and the idea received [[25:95|AIH 4-2]]. You have communicated when the learner understood the idea the way you intended, and communication is a two-way process [[25:94|AIH 4-1]]. It has three elements, each dependent on the others [[25:95|AIH 4-2]]:

head: Element
Who or what
What makes it work
rows: Source
Sender, speaker, writer, encoder, transmitter or instructor [[25:95|AIH 4-2]]

Three factors: select language meaningful to the receiver (acronyms like ILS, TCAS or TAWS fail with a new learner pilot); be confident and show that the message is important and the receiver needs it; and use accurate, up-to-date, stimulating material, since out-of-date information costs credibility [[25:95|AIH 4-2]]
Symbols
Simple oral, visual or tactile codes: words, gestures, facial expressions [[25:95|AIH 4-2]]
Combine them into meaningful wholes. Use several channels (visual, auditory and kinesthetic); for motor skills, touch is added as the learner practices [[25:95|AIH 4-2]]
Receiver
Listener, reader, decoder or learner [[25:96|AIH 4-3]]

Communication succeeds only in relation to the receiver's reaction: understanding plus a change in behavior as the source intended. Know the receiver's abilities, attitudes and experiences [[25:96|AIH 4-3]]

body.p: In the AIH's opening example, Carol prepares a learner for his first tailwheel flight. She explains precession, then moves a model propeller under a desk lamp so its shadow shows the propeller's pitch change as the tail comes up [[25:94|AIH 4-1]]. The AIH names the model propeller and desk lamp as symbols [[25:95|AIH 4-2]]: the words carried the idea, and the model and its shadow carried it again on another channel. The trim example works the same way: instead of only telling the learner to trim, move the trim wheel while the learner holds the attitude so the change in control pressure is felt, and explain what is felt at the same time [[25:95|AIH 4-2]].

**Know the receiver.** Consider how familiar the learner is with aviation and how developed the motor skills are [[25:96|AIH 4-3]]. Be aware of cultural differences without overreacting or assuming: a college degree does not guarantee rapid advancement, so base your style on what the learner knows about the aviation subject being taught [[25:97|AIH 4-4]]. Attitudes may show resistance, willingness or passive neutrality, so a varied approach works best, and the typical aviation learner is an adult with motivation, prior knowledge, life experience and decision-making skills [[25:97|AIH 4-4]].

callout.text: Application for instrument training: brief the cross-check with a panel picture and point to each instrument as you name it; in the airplane, let the learner feel the pitch change while you name the instrument that shows it. Several channels, one idea [[25:95|AIH 4-2]].

check.q: You brief a brand-new instrument learner on 'RAIM, LPV and the TAA,' and she nods. Which source factor did you miss, and what is the fix?
check.a: Selecting language that is meaningful to the receiver: acronyms the learner does not know make effective communication difficult if not impossible [[25:95|AIH 4-2]]. Define each term or use plain words, then check understanding through feedback [[25:96|AIH 4-3]].

body.p: The source and the receiver depend on a two-way flow of symbols. The source needs feedback from the receiver to tailor the communication, and the source gives feedback to the receiver to reinforce the desired responses [[25:95|AIH 4-2]].

**Feedback from the learner.** Monitor it constantly to catch misunderstandings. Periodically ask the learner to explain new information while you present it, then change your symbols as needed [[25:96|AIH 4-3]]. In AIH Figure 4-2 the learner takes 'stall' to mean the engine quitting, and the instructor catches it from the reply and clarifies [[25:96|AIH 4-3]].

**Feedback to the learner.** Praise builds self-confidence and reinforces favorable behavior. Use negative feedback carefully: only in private, as a description of actual performance, in a nonjudgmental manner. Telling a maintenance learner that a safety wire installation is not satisfactory is fine; calling the work careless can harm the learner's feeling of self-worth [[25:96|AIH 4-3]].

**Positive exchange of flight controls** is the AIH's clearest closed-loop procedure. Numerous accidents have occurred from a lack of communication or misunderstanding about who had control, particularly between learners and instructors, so the preflight briefing should cover the three-step exchange [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]. A visual check is recommended, and the learner keeps flying until the instructor says 'I have the flight controls' [[25:179|AIH 9-9]]. When necessary, the instructor takes the controls and calmly announces it; anxious learners can be incredibly strong, and nothing is gained by fighting the learner for control [[25:179|AIH 9-9]]. The PTS lists positive exchange of flight controls among the areas the evaluator emphasizes and recommends the same three steps [[FAA-S-8081-9E:10|PTS Special Emphasis Areas]] [[FAA-S-8081-9E:16|PTS Positive Exchange of Flight Controls]].

callout.text: Application: use the same loop for any instrument instruction that matters. Say it, hear it read back, then watch it happen on the instruments. The AIH says instructors and learners confirm a message by observing its effect [[25:99|AIH 4-6]].

check.q: Your learner hands you the airplane by saying 'You have the flight controls' and lets go before you answer. What went wrong?
check.a: The exchange is three steps, and when returning control the learner follows the same procedure and keeps flying until the instructor says 'I have the flight controls' [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].

chunks.title: Barriers I: experience, symbols and abstractions

body.p: **Barriers of effective communication.** The nature of language and the way it is used often lead to misunderstandings. The AIH names four barriers: lack of common experience, confusion between the symbol and the symbolized object, overuse of abstractions, and external factors [[25:97|AIH 4-4]].

**Lack of common experience** is probably the greatest single barrier. Communication is effective only to the extent that the physical, mental and emotional experiences of the people are similar [[25:97|AIH 4-4]]. Words do not carry meaning the way a truck carries bricks; they are only stimuli that arouse a response, and the learner's own past experience decides that response. Since experience forms vocabulary, speak the learner's language, and spend time making sure needed terms are understood [[25:97|AIH 4-4]]. 'Time the magnetos' has nothing to do with a stopwatch, and 'tractor' means different things to a farmer, a trucker and a pilot [[25:98|AIH 4-5]]. When you or the learner use English as a second language, note whether it creates a significant barrier; if there is reasonable doubt about a learner's ability to communicate in English at an appropriate level, the AIH points you to AC 60-28 for guidance [[25:98|AIH 4-5]].

**Confusion between the symbol and the symbolized object** happens when a word is confused with what it is meant to represent. Calling an AMT a 'mechanic' may conjure up someone laboring over an automobile. Allow for possible misinterpretation and choose words that represent what you intend [[25:98|AIH 4-5]].

**Overuse of abstractions.** Abstract words are general, not specific: 'aircraft' may bring up an airplane, a helicopter or an airship, and even 'airplane' can mean anything from a Boeing 777 to a Piper Cub [[25:98|AIH 4-5]]. Abstractions are sometimes necessary, as with aerodynamics, but link them to specific experiences through examples and illustrations [[25:99|AIH 4-6]]. On an approach that is going badly, 'take appropriate measures' may not get the action you want; 'go around' has the same meaning to both of you [[25:99|AIH 4-6]].

callout.text: Application: in the airplane, turn abstractions into instrument names and actions. Not 'watch your altitude,' but 'altimeter: 100 feet high, ease the nose down.' The concrete version says what to look at and what to do [[25:99|AIH 4-6]].

check.q: On vectors to final your learner drifts high and you say only 'fix it.' She grips the yoke harder and the heading wanders. Which barrier is this, and what should you have said?
check.a: Overuse of abstractions: 'fix it' is general and calls up no specific action. Use concrete, specific terms that name what to check and what to do [[25:99|AIH 4-6]].

chunks.title: Barriers II: external factors and interference

body.p: **External factors** are barriers outside the instructor's control. They may be physiological, environmental or psychological, and you consider their effects and mitigate them where possible [[25:99|AIH 4-6]].

head: Factor
Examples
What you can do
rows: Physiological
Hearing loss, injury, physical illness or another congenital condition [[25:99|AIH 4-6]]
Adapt the presentation: put off the lesson until the learner is over an illness, or use a seat cushion so the learner sits properly [[25:99|AIH 4-6]]
Physiological: multitasking
People can handle two simple, low-level tasks at once, but a higher-level task needs full concentration, and adding even a simple activity reduces comprehension and recall of both [[25:99|AIH 4-6]]
Application: do not teach a new idea while the learner copies a clearance or intercepts the final approach course
Environmental
Noise in many light aircraft, which can also damage hearing over time; vibration in rotary wing aircraft [[25:99|AIH 4-6]]
Headsets and an intercom; without an intercom, earplugs, which also clarify speaker output [[25:99|AIH 4-6]]
Psychological
How instructor and learner feel at the time. Lack of commitment, fear of the situation or mistrust between them disrupts communication [[25:99|AIH 4-6]]
Application: build trust before the hard lessons; a calm, pleasant manner puts the learner at ease [[25:167|AIH 8-9]]

body.p: **Interference.** The message gets disrupted, truncated or added to somewhere in the sequence, while both people may believe it arrived intact. Noise and other factors may distort the message, and psychological factors also interfere. Instructors and learners confirm the message by observing its effect, and more feedback and confirmation reduce the harm [[25:99|AIH 4-6]].

**One barrier, two names.** The text's fourth barrier is external factors, and it treats interference separately [[25:97|AIH 4-4]] [[25:99|AIH 4-6]]. Figure 4-3 lists interference as one of the four instead [[25:97|AIH 4-4]], and the glossary defines interference as barriers caused by physiological, environmental and psychological factors outside the instructor's control [[25:212|AIH G-4]]. Teach the four from the text, and say that the figure and glossary call the fourth one interference.

callout.text: The sterile flight deck rule, 14 CFR 121.542, requires airline flight crewmembers to refrain from nonessential activities during critical phases of flight. The AIH says the idea holds true for the entire aviation community and that the flight instructor should teach and model it [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].

check.q: Your learner nods at your in-flight explanation in a hot, noisy trainer with a weak intercom. Why is the nod not enough?
check.a: Noise is an environmental external factor, and interference can distort a message while both people believe it arrived intact. Confirm it by observing the effect of the message, with more feedback and confirmation [[25:99|AIH 4-6]].

body.p: **Developing communication skills.** They do not occur automatically. They come from experience that begins with role playing during instructor training, continues during actual instruction and grows with additional training [[25:99|AIH 4-6]].

head: Skill
What the AIH says
Instrument instructor use (application)
rows: Role playing

The learner gets a general description of a situation and applies a new skill in a role. A flight instructor plays the learner pilot, duplicates known learner responses and critiques the applicant; a non-threatening setting helps a new instructor find a comfortable style [[25:100|AIH 4-7]]. As emphasis on SBT grows, so does the importance of role playing [[25:100|AIH 4-7]]
Have a CFII play a learner who fixates on partial panel and blames ATC; brief, talk through and debrief, then trade seats
Instructional communication

Instruction has taken place when you explain a procedure and then see the desired response. Teach what you know well; use your own experiences, such as moving from IMC to visual cues on an approach, but avoid 'there I was' war stories; check whether good performance was retained or a one-time event; teach how and why [[25:100|AIH 4-7]]
After an approach is flown well once, see it again on a later lesson before you call it learned
Listening
Know your learners by being a good listener, and self-evaluate. Listening is 'hearing with comprehension' [[25:101|AIH 4-8]]
Use the instructor tools below, and teach learners to listen
Questioning

Ask focused, open-ended questions; closed-ended ones evaluate only rote learning. Fit each question to the learner's ability, experience and stage of training, keep it to one idea, and make it a suitable challenge [[25:103|AIH 4-10]]
Not 'Do you understand the hold?' but 'How will you enter this hold?'
Instructional enhancement
An instructor never stops learning; the more you know, the better you convey it. Be ready to answer beyond the lesson, but present what fits the learner's level [[25:103|AIH 4-10]]
Know the avionics and procedures more deeply than the lesson needs

body.p: **Listening tools.** For instructors, Figure 4-5 lists: do not interrupt, do not judge, think before answering, be close enough to hear, watch nonverbal behavior, beware of biases, look for underlying feelings, concentrate, avoid rehearsing answers while listening, and do not insist on the last word [[25:101|AIH 4-8]]. For learners, Figure 4-6 shows the steps to effective listening: be ready to listen, listen to understand rather than refute, be responsible for listening, take notes, be emotionally calm, listen for main ideas and guard against daydreaming [[25:102|AIH 4-9]]. A learner instrument pilot who knows the format of a typical clearance can build his own abbreviations and copy it in a form useful for readback and for flying it [[25:102|AIH 4-9]].

**Confirming understanding.** Paraphrasing shows the learner what the learner's statement meant to you, so the learner can correct or expand it. Perception checking states your perception of the learner's behavior so the learner can clarify the feelings behind it. Phrase questions to focus the learner on decision-making and judgment [[25:103|AIH 4-10]]. Remind learners that emotions interfere with listening; if a topic arouses fear, allay it or prepare the learner to listen first [[25:101|AIH 4-8]].

callout.text: Application: in the debrief, ask an open-ended question, listen without interrupting, paraphrase what you heard, and check your perception of how the learner feels before you give your own view [[25:101|AIH 4-8]] [[25:103|AIH 4-10]].

check.q: Rewrite this debrief question to fit the AIH guidance: 'How and why would you enter this hold, and when do you slow down?'
check.a: Split it. Effective questions center on one idea, limited to who, what, when, where, why or how, not a combination [[25:103|AIH 4-10]]. Ask 'How will you enter this hold?', then follow up with 'Why that entry?' and 'When will you slow down?'

chunks.title: Explaining this Task to the examiner

body.p: This is a knowledge Task. The objective is to exhibit instructional knowledge by describing, and instructional knowledge means your explanations follow the teaching procedures and techniques of the Aviation Instructor's Handbook [[FAA-S-8081-9E:23|PTS I.B]] [[FAA-S-8081-9E:10|PTS Use of the PTS]]. Evaluators are told to test application and correlation and to use scenario-based questions when possible [[FAA-S-8081-9E:14|PTS Evaluator Responsibility]], so expect 'Here is a learner who...' more than 'List the...'.
A four-part answer works for each item (application):

bullets: 1. Name it in the PTS words and in the current AIH words.
2. Give the AIH list or definition.
4. Say what you would do with that learner on the next lesson.

head: Item
Sample opening line (application)
rows: Control of human behavior

'Behavior follows perception and needs. A threatened learner's attention narrows to the threat [[25:59|AIH 3-8]], so I steer behavior with positive motivation and difficult but possible goals [[25:35|AIH 2-2]] [[25:43|AIH 2-10]].'
Human needs
'Maslow ranked them, but the AIH says the order matters little. I verify most needs are met with a pre-assessment, then focus the learner on the lesson [[25:39|AIH 2-6]].'
Defense mechanisms

'They are unconscious and distort reality, and they relieve symptoms, not causes [[25:42|AIH 2-9]] [[25:44|AIH 2-11]]. I discuss the facts to restore motivation and self-confidence [[25:45|AIH 2-12]].'
Practical psychologist

'I analyze each learner's personality, thinking and ability and adapt my methods [[25:159|AIH 8-1]]. If I suspect a serious problem, I get an unbiased evaluation flight and withhold endorsements if warranted [[25:49|AIH 2-16]].'
Basic elements
'Source, symbols and receiver, with feedback both ways. It worked only if the learner reacts with understanding and changes behavior as I intended [[25:95|AIH 4-2]] [[25:96|AIH 4-3]].'
Barriers
'Lack of common experience, symbol confusion, abstractions and external factors. I confirm each key message by its effect [[25:97|AIH 4-4]] [[25:99|AIH 4-6]].'
Developing skills
'Role playing, instructional communication, listening, questioning and never-ending learning [[25:100|AIH 4-7]] [[25:101|AIH 4-8]] [[25:103|AIH 4-10]].'

body.p: **Role-play is part of the test.** During the flight portion the evaluator acts as a student during selected maneuvers, oral questions may come at any time, and positive exchange of flight controls is among the areas the evaluator emphasizes [[FAA-S-8081-9E:13|PTS Evaluator Responsibility]] [[FAA-S-8081-9E:14|PTS Evaluator Responsibility]]. Application: if the 'student' blames the chart or the controller, show this Task by how you respond, not by naming the mechanism aloud.

check.q: The examiner, playing your student, blames the 'confusing' approach chart for a missed step-down fix. How do you show this Task in your response?
check.a: Recognize a likely defense mechanism, such as projection or rationalization [[25:43|AIH 2-10]], without labeling it aloud; discuss the facts privately and without judgment [[25:96|AIH 4-3]]; aim to restore motivation and self-confidence [[25:45|AIH 2-12]]; and confirm the fix with an open-ended question [[25:103|AIH 4-10]].
