scenario.title: The approach that fell apart
scenario.setup: Rachel is a 41-year-old private pilot with 280 hours who runs a busy hospital department. She is halfway through her instrument rating in a Cessna 172 with a glass flight deck, and her checkride is already booked. Her employer has just announced layoffs. She arrives 20 minutes late for an evening lesson, says she worked through lunch, and wants to 'get the approaches done.' On the last lesson she flew good holds, but when ATC amended her clearance on the first approach she fell behind, fixated on the heading display and descended 200 feet below a step-down altitude before you said 'watch it.' In the debrief she said the controller 'talked way too fast' and the chart was 'badly designed,' and she answered 'yes' when you asked, 'Do you understand what happened?'

questions.q: Before you go to the airplane, what do you check, and what does the AIH say decides whether today's lesson can work?
questions.a: Run a pre-assessment to verify she is physically and mentally ready [[25:39|AIH 2-6]]. She skipped lunch, and a hungry learner's focus of perception is on the need, not the lesson [[25:38|AIH 2-5]]; the IMSAFE stress item asks about pressure from the job [[25:12|AIH 1-8]]. Verify that most of her needs are met before you focus her on the lesson [[25:39|AIH 2-6]]; if they are not, change the plan.

questions.q: What are her comments about the controller and the chart most likely to be, and how do you respond?
questions.a: Placing the blame for her own error on others is projection, and sincerely believed, plausible excuses are rationalization [[25:43|AIH 2-10]]. Both are unconscious and relieve symptoms, not causes [[25:44|AIH 2-11]]. Discuss the facts with common sense, in private and without judgment, aiming to restore her motivation and self-confidence [[25:45|AIH 2-12]] [[25:96|AIH 4-3]].

questions.q: How do the layoffs and the booked checkride bear on what you are seeing?
questions.a: Outside worries affect training and cannot be separated from it; you are not responsible for them but cannot ignore them, so key instruction to her interests and divert her attention to the task [[25:46|AIH 2-13]]. A stressful event is the usual cause of excessive reliance on defense mechanisms, and an inability to concentrate is one of the signs [[25:44|AIH 2-11]]. Watch, talk with her, and recommend a professional counselor only if the signs point to a deep problem [[25:45|AIH 2-12]].

questions.q: She fixated and went low after the amended clearance. What explains it, and how should the next lesson differ?
questions.a: Threat narrows the perceptual field onto the threat [[25:59|AIH 3-8]], and an instrument learner anticipating routing changes can become too anxious to listen to and process the new route [[25:101|AIH 4-8]]. Fixation can also come from uncertainty about interpretation or control [[23:146|IFH 6-13]]. Treat the anxiety as normal and, as the AIH advises for anxiety-producing maneuvers, introduce clearance changes with care so she knows what to expect [[25:45|AIH 2-12]], and build her clearance copying around the clearance format and her own abbreviations [[25:102|AIH 4-9]].

questions.q: What was wrong with 'watch it,' and what should you say next time?
questions.a: It is an abstraction that names no instrument and no action; use concrete, specific terms instead [[25:99|AIH 4-6]]. Application: 'Altimeter, 200 feet low: climb back to the step-down altitude.' If you need to take the airplane, use the three-step positive exchange of flight controls [[25:178|AIH 9-8]] [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].

questions.q: How do you confirm she really understood the debrief?
questions.a: 'Do you understand?' is closed-ended and checks only rote learning. Ask focused, open-ended questions about one idea at a time, and use paraphrasing and perception checking [[25:103|AIH 4-10]]. Instruction has taken place only when you see the desired response, and you then check whether good performance is retained or was a one-time event [[25:100|AIH 4-7]].

skills.do: Describe human behavior aloud the way an examiner expects: control of human behavior (perception, needs, motivation and goals), human needs and the pre-assessment, defense mechanisms with an instrument example of each, and your role as a practical psychologist, including what you do about a seriously abnormal learner.
skills.practice: Pick one instrument learner you have flown with, or invent one, and explain in three minutes what drove that learner's behavior and what you changed, naming the AIH ideas you used [[25:34|AIH 2-1]] [[25:39|AIH 2-6]] [[25:160|AIH 8-2]]. Then have a study partner read you eight learner quotes and name each defense mechanism and your response [[25:42|AIH 2-9]] [[25:43|AIH 2-10]] [[25:44|AIH 2-11]] [[25:45|AIH 2-12]].

skills.do: Describe effective communication: the three basic elements and the feedback loop, the four barriers with a fix for each, and how you develop communication skills, using short, concrete examples from instrument training.
skills.practice: Role-play a hood lesson with another applicant: one plays an anxious learner, the other briefs, talks through and debriefs; then trade roles and critique each other [[25:100|AIH 4-7]]. Record your in-flight calls and replace every abstraction with a concrete instrument-and-action call [[25:99|AIH 4-6]], and rewrite every closed-ended debrief question as an open-ended one [[25:103|AIH 4-10]].

quiz.q: On his first steep turns under the hood your learner stares at the altimeter and stops cross-checking. You warn him sharply that he will fail the stage check if this goes on. According to the AIH, what is the likely effect of the warning?
options: His cross-check speeds up because the threat focuses him
His perceptual field narrows further onto the threat
None, since perception depends only on the senses
He moves into System 2 thinking and analyzes it
quiz.why: Fear narrows the perceptual field, and threats of unsatisfactory reports or reprisals may seem logical but are not effective psychologically [[25:59|AIH 3-8]]. Perception is more than the senses: it also involves giving meaning to sensations [[25:58|AIH 3-7]].

quiz.q: With which learners does the AIH say negative motivation may be used?
options: Timid learners who need a firm push
Any learner within a month of the checkride
Learners who have hit a learning plateau
Only the most overconfident and impulsive
quiz.why: Negative motivation should be avoided with all but the most overconfident and impulsive learners [[25:37|AIH 2-4]]. Too much criticism may discourage a timid person [[25:159|AIH 8-1]], and a plateau calls for reassurance that learning seldom proceeds at a constant pace [[25:38|AIH 2-5]].

quiz.q: Your learner flies the RNAV (GPS) approach at her home field well. At a new airport she briefs a similar-looking approach in seconds and misses a step-down fix. In Kahneman's two-system model, what happened?
options: System 1 assumed it was as simple as the last one
System 2 took over and slowed her briefing down
A defense mechanism distorted how she read the chart
She showed a normal fight or flight reaction
quiz.why: System 1 is fast and automatic and can lead to poor decisions by assuming a task is as simple as similar past ones [[25:41|AIH 2-8]]. The AIH names reusing a recent solution on a task that only looks similar as a learner pitfall [[25:42|AIH 2-9]]. System 2 is the slow, deliberate thinking she skipped.

quiz.q: Your learner arrives for an evening approach lesson straight from work. He skipped lunch and dinner but is eager to fly. What does the AIH guidance on human needs support?
options: Fly as planned, since the order of needs does not matter
Cancel, since each level must first be met 100 percent
Deal with the need before you focus him on the lesson
Fly a review lesson, since review needs no attention
quiz.why: A hungry learner's focus of perception is on satisfying the need, not on the instructor [[25:38|AIH 2-5]]. Needs need not be met 100 percent and their order has little effect, but you verify most needs are met before focusing the learner on the lesson [[25:39|AIH 2-6]]. The 100 percent rule is Maslow's claim, which the AIH says does not hold [[25:38|AIH 2-5]].

quiz.q: Your new instrument learner just moved to the area, knows no one at the airport and seems withdrawn. Which need fits best, and what does the AIH say to do?
options: Esteem: praise her flying in front of others
Belonging: help her feel at ease at the school
Security: stress the safety record of the fleet
Physiological: confirm she has eaten and slept
quiz.why: Belonging is about overcoming loneliness and alienation. Learners are usually out of their normal surroundings, so the need is more pronounced; help new learners feel at ease and reinforce their decision to fly [[25:40|AIH 2-7]].

quiz.q: Which two properties does the AIH say defense mechanisms share?
options: They are deliberate and always harmful
They fix the underlying cause and ease the anxiety
They appear unconsciously and distort reality
They show up only after a major personal crisis
quiz.why: They often appear unconsciously and tend to distort, transform or falsify reality [[25:42|AIH 2-9]]. They relieve symptoms, not causes, and most are normal; a personal crisis is the usual cause only of excessive reliance on them [[25:44|AIH 2-11]].

quiz.q: After a weak stage check, your learner says, and clearly believes, that the holiday schedule left him no time to prepare. He does not mention the two training device sessions he skipped. Which defense mechanism fits best?
options: Projection
Displacement
Reaction formation
Rationalization
quiz.why: Rationalization justifies otherwise unacceptable actions with plausible excuses the person sincerely believes, like the AIH's learner who blames lack of time but skipped the study group and practice quiz [[25:43|AIH 2-10]]. Projection places the blame on another person [[25:43|AIH 2-10]].

quiz.q: You believe a learner's defense mechanisms are hiding a real problem since his divorce. What does the AIH say is the main objective when you discuss it with him?
options: Restore his motivation and self-confidence
Get him to admit which mechanism he uses
Diagnose the problem before the next flight
Halt all training until the crisis is over
quiz.why: Use common sense and discuss the problem; the main objective should be to restore motivation and self-confidence, and severe cases call for a professional counselor [[25:45|AIH 2-12]]. Mechanisms are unconscious and not subject to normal conscious checks [[25:44|AIH 2-11]], so an admission is not the goal.

quiz.q: Your fast learner flies approaches well and has started to shrug off small errors. What does the AIH suggest?
options: Invent a few faults so that he stays careful
Ease off, since few errors mean he is ready
Raise the standard of performance each lesson
Move him straight on to the practical test
quiz.why: Fast learners may assume error correction is unimportant and become overconfident. Constantly raise the standard of performance each lesson, but do not invent deficiencies, because unfair criticism destroys the learner's confidence in the instructor [[25:160|AIH 8-2]].

quiz.q: You fail the attitude indicator on a practice approach. Your learner covers it, moves to the standby instruments and keeps flying calmly and precisely. How does the AIH classify this?
options: An abnormal reaction, since she showed no anxiety
A normal reaction: rapid and exact, within training
Denial of the danger that the failure represents
Fantasy, an escape from the real situation
quiz.why: Normal individuals respond rapidly and exactly within the limits of their experience and training, think rationally and act rapidly; many responses are automatic, which is why emergencies are trained in advance [[25:48|AIH 2-15]]. An abnormal response is absent or inadequate, random or illogical, or more than the situation calls for [[25:48|AIH 2-15]].

quiz.q: Starting a ground lesson, you sigh and say, 'You will probably never need this, but the FAA makes us cover it.' Which source factor are you working against?
options: Selecting language the receiver understands
Using accurate and up-to-date material
Combining symbols into meaningful wholes
Showing that the message is important
quiz.why: Communicators reveal their self-image, their view of the ideas and their feelings toward the receivers, so they should be confident and show that the message is important and that the receivers need it [[25:95|AIH 4-2]]. Language and accurate, up-to-date, stimulating material are the other two source factors; combining symbols belongs to the symbols element [[25:95|AIH 4-2]].

quiz.q: Which three characteristics of the receiver does the AIH say an instructor needs to understand?
options: Abilities, attitudes and experiences
Needs, motives and defense mechanisms
Age, education and cultural background
Hearing, vision and the sense of touch
quiz.why: The three characteristics of receivers are abilities, attitudes and experiences [[25:96|AIH 4-3]]. The AIH warns against assumptions based on education or cultural differences [[25:97|AIH 4-4]].

quiz.q: Your learner has never flown an instrument approach. You explain 'step-down fix' and 'MDA,' and she nods. In the AIH's view, why may the meaning not have reached her?
options: Aviation terms are abstractions that should never be used
Kinesthetic learners cannot learn from words
Words only stir a response built on her own experience
She confused a spoken symbol with a printed one
quiz.why: Words do not transfer meanings at all; they are stimuli that arouse a response, and the learner's past experience with the words and the things they refer to decides it. That is lack of common experience, probably the greatest single barrier [[25:97|AIH 4-4]]. Abstractions are sometimes necessary if linked to examples [[25:99|AIH 4-6]].

quiz.q: In the AIH's section on instructional communication, when has instruction taken place?
options: When you have covered every item in the lesson plan
When you explain it and then see the desired response
When the learner tells you she understands it
When the learner passes a written quiz on it
quiz.why: Instruction has taken place when the instructor explains a procedure and then determines that the learner exhibits the desired response; you also check whether the performance was retained or a one-time event [[25:100|AIH 4-7]].

final_quiz.q: Which of the AIH's three ways of defining human behavior explains why you plan differently for a 19-year-old and a 50-year-old learner?
options: The typical life course of humans
The result of attempts to satisfy needs
A product of factors causing predictable acts
The output of fast, automatic System 1
final_quiz.why: The life-course definition says that as people mature, their mode of action moves from dependency to self-direction, so the learner's age affects how you design the curriculum [[25:34|AIH 2-1]]. System 1 comes from Kahneman's model of human nature, not from the definitions [[25:41|AIH 2-8]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner holds altitude within the lesson's completion standard in a hold, but you tell him it is not good enough because he was 20 feet off for a moment. What does the AIH say such demands do?
options: Raise his standard and speed his progress
Nothing at all, if he is a fast learner
Build his esteem through a hard challenge
Discourage him and diminish his effort
final_quiz.why: Impossible or unreasonable goals discourage the learner, diminish effort and retard learning [[25:44|AIH 2-11]], and motivation declines when the learner believes the demands are unreasonable [[25:43|AIH 2-10]]. Even with fast learners, deficiencies should not be invented [[25:160|AIH 8-2]].

final_quiz.q: How does the AIH say you verify, before a lesson, that a learner's human needs have been met?
options: A short written quiz on the last lesson
Asking the learner to rate her motivation
A thorough pre-assessment
Watching her first maneuver of the day
final_quiz.why: To satisfy the law of readiness, verify that the learner's needs have been met with a thorough pre-assessment before beginning the lesson; it should verify whether the learner is physically and mentally ready [[25:39|AIH 2-6]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner is uneasy about her first unusual attitude recoveries under the hood. Which need is involved, and what does the AIH tell you to do?
options: Esteem: praise her past successes first
Security: ease her into the region with care
Belonging: say every learner feels this way
Cognitive: give the full aerodynamics lecture
final_quiz.why: Security needs are about keeping oneself from harm; a learner who does not feel safe cannot concentrate, and the instructor should ease the learner into feared flight regions carefully [[25:39|AIH 2-6]]. Introduce such maneuvers so learners know what to expect [[25:45|AIH 2-12]].

final_quiz.q: During her first full stall an anxious learner tenses, breathes fast and freezes on the yoke. Which kind of defense mechanism is this, and what does the AIH suggest?
options: Biological: teach the maneuver in stages
Psychological: refer her to a counselor
Repression: avoid stalls until the fear fades
Denial: replay the video until she accepts it
final_quiz.why: Fight or flight is the biological defense mechanism. For the anxious learner in stalls, the AIH says to take the procedure apart, demonstrate each stage and let the learner practice the stages in realistic scenarios [[25:42|AIH 2-9]]. Counselors are for severe psychological cases [[25:45|AIH 2-12]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner struggles with partial panel work but steers every debrief toward how smooth his landings are. Which defense mechanism is this?
options: Rationalization
Reaction formation
Compensation
Projection
final_quiz.why: Compensation counterbalances a perceived weakness by emphasizing strength in another area [[25:43|AIH 2-10]]. Rationalization would be a sincere excuse, and projection would put the blame on someone else [[25:43|AIH 2-10]].

final_quiz.q: The AIH says an aviation instructor serves 'in some ways' as a practical psychologist. How does it say you meet that responsibility?
options: Earn a counseling credential before you teach
Give each learner a personality type test
Diagnose problems before signing any solo
Know the FOI and carefully analyze each learner
final_quiz.why: You meet it by becoming familiar and conversant in the fundamentals of instructing and through a careful analysis of and continuing interest in learners [[25:160|AIH 8-2]]. A flight instructor does not need to be a certified psychologist [[25:45|AIH 2-12]], and teaching by personality type is controversial [[25:34|AIH 2-1]].

final_quiz.q: You come to believe a learner may have a serious psychological problem. What is the first step the AIH lists?
options: A solo endorsement limited to the traffic pattern only
An evaluation flight by an instructor who does not know her
A report to the local FSDO before she may fly again
More flights with you so you can gather evidence
final_quiz.why: Arrange for another instructor who is not acquainted with the learner to conduct an evaluation flight, then confer; if you both still suspect a serious deficiency, withhold solo endorsements and practical test recommendations [[25:49|AIH 2-16]]. You also have a responsibility to refrain from instructing that learner [[25:49|AIH 2-16]].

final_quiz.q: In the debrief room, with two other learners present, you need to tell your learner he went 300 feet below the missed approach altitude. How does the AIH say to give this feedback?
options: In private, describing what happened
In front of the others, so all can learn from it
In private, telling him plainly it was careless
In writing only, so there is a record of it
final_quiz.why: Use negative feedback only in private, delivered as a description of actual performance in a nonjudgmental manner; calling work careless can harm the learner's self-worth [[25:96|AIH 4-3]].

final_quiz.q: Figure 9-8 shows the three spoken steps of a positive exchange of flight controls. What else does the AIH recommend during the exchange?
options: A shake of the yoke so the other pilot feels it
A pause of a few seconds after each spoken call
A callout of airspeed and altitude at handover
A visual check that the other pilot has the controls
final_quiz.why: During this procedure a visual check is recommended to see that the other person actually has the flight controls, and the learner keeps flying until the instructor says 'I have the flight controls' [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].

final_quiz.q: Your ground lesson on aerodynamics uses general terms like lift and drag that apply to every aircraft. What does the AIH say about abstractions like these?
options: They should always be avoided in teaching
They help, if linked to specific examples
They are fine, since every pilot shares them
They suit only learners with a degree
final_quiz.why: Abstractions should be avoided in most cases, but some, like aerodynamics, are necessary and useful; link them with specific experiences through examples and illustrations [[25:99|AIH 4-6]].

final_quiz.q: While your learner copies a reroute clearance, you start explaining a new idea about the approach. What does the research the AIH cites on multitasking predict?
options: Both go fine, since both are simple tasks
The clearance suffers, but the idea sticks
Her comprehension and recall of both drop
Recall improves from the extra stimulation
final_quiz.why: People can handle two simple, low-level tasks at once, but a higher-level task needs concentration, and adding even a simple activity diminishes comprehension and recall of both [[25:99|AIH 4-6]].

final_quiz.q: Your instrument learner tries to copy every word of each clearance and misses the altitude. What does the AIH recommend?
options: Learn the clearance format and use her own abbreviations
Ask ATC to read every clearance more slowly
Write every word first, then sort out the meaning
Skip writing and rely on reading it back
final_quiz.why: Copying a clearance word for word is very difficult. By knowing the format of a typical clearance, learner instrument pilots can develop their own abbreviations and copy it in a useful form for readback and for flying it [[25:102|AIH 4-9]].

final_quiz.q: Which debrief question best fits the AIH's guidance on effective questions?
options: Do you understand the hold entry now?
How and why will you enter, and when do you slow?
You would use a teardrop entry here, right?
How will you enter the hold at this fix?
final_quiz.why: Ask focused, open-ended questions, often starting with how or why; keep each to one idea, not a combination of who, what, when, where, why or how [[25:103|AIH 4-10]]. Yes/no and leading questions are closed-ended and test only rote learning [[25:103|AIH 4-10]].

final_quiz.q: After the controller changes her route, you tell your learner, 'You seem tense since that reroute.' Which AIH technique is this?
options: Paraphrasing
Listening for main ideas
Perception checking
Role playing
final_quiz.why: Perception checking gets to the learner's feelings by stating the perceptions the instructor has of the behavior, which the learner can then clarify. Paraphrasing restates what the learner's statement meant to you [[25:103|AIH 4-10]].

final_quiz.q: You praise your learner's checklist use each time she does it right, and it becomes a habit. Which idea in the AIH does this reflect most directly?
options: Constructivism: building her own knowledge
Behaviorism: reinforcement by the instructor
Kahneman: a shift to slow System 2 thinking
Maslow: meeting the need for self-actualization
final_quiz.why: In modern education, behaviorism stresses having a behavior positively reinforced by someone other than the learner who shapes or controls what is learned; in aviation training, the instructor provides the reinforcement [[25:54|AIH 3-3]]. The law of effect agrees: behaviors with satisfying outcomes tend to be repeated [[25:63|AIH 3-12]].

takeaways: The PTS lists FAA-H-8083-9; answer in the current 9B's words and connect them to the PTS item names.
Behavior follows perception and needs: threat narrows attention, while positive motivation and difficult but possible goals steer effort.
Maslow's order matters little; a pre-assessment that confirms most needs are met is what counts.
Defense mechanisms are unconscious and distort reality; discuss the facts calmly to restore motivation and self-confidence.
A practical psychologist analyzes each learner and adapts; for a possibly serious problem, get an unbiased evaluation flight and withhold endorsements if warranted.
Communication worked only if the learner reacts with understanding and changes behavior as you intended.
Four barriers: lack of common experience, symbol confusion, abstractions and external factors. Confirm key messages by their effect.
Develop the skills: role play, teach how and why, listen, and ask open-ended, one-idea questions.
cfi_notes: How it is tested: the evaluator must select at least Tasks E, F and G and one other task in Area I [[FAA-S-8081-9E:23|PTS Area I NOTE]], so this Task is tested when it is chosen as that other one. The verb is 'describing', and evaluators are told to test application and correlation with scenario-based questions when possible [[FAA-S-8081-9E:14|PTS Evaluator Responsibility]].

Who meets Area I: it is part of the initial flight instructor instrument certificate, but in the PTS table for adding an instrument instructor rating to a flight instructor certificate, Area I is marked N (not required) for every certificate and rating held [[FAA-S-8081-9E:18|PTS Addition of an Instrument Instructor Rating]]. This course is also preparation for the fundamentals of instructing knowledge test [[12:48|AC 61-65K A.45]].

Terms: 'control of human behavior' is not a heading in FAA-H-8083-9B. Answer from what drives behavior [[25:34|AIH 2-1]], reinforcement by the instructor in behaviorism [[25:54|AIH 3-3]], perception and threat [[25:59|AIH 3-8]] and motivation [[25:35|AIH 2-2]], and say so if asked. 'Practical psychologist' does appear, in Chapter 8 [[25:160|AIH 8-2]].

Source conflict, barriers: the text lists four barriers ending with external factors and treats interference separately [[25:97|AIH 4-4]] [[25:99|AIH 4-6]]; Figure 4-3 lists interference as one of the four [[25:97|AIH 4-4]]; and the glossary's communication meaning of interference matches the text's external factors [[25:212|AIH G-4]]. Teach the text and mention the figure.

Source conflict, Maslow: the AIH says Maslow's hierarchy holds that each level must be met 100 percent before the next, and that self-actualization is activated 'then and only then' [[25:38|AIH 2-5]] [[25:40|AIH 2-7]], but also that studies give the hierarchy little support and that order has little effect on learning [[25:38|AIH 2-5]] [[25:39|AIH 2-6]]. Present the model as Maslow's and the AIH's conclusion as the guidance. Figure 2-3 shows five levels; the glossary adds cognitive and aesthetic [[25:211|AIH G-3]].

Same word, two meanings: repression is a defense mechanism [[25:42|AIH 2-9]] and also a theory of forgetting [[25:89|AIH 3-38]] [[25:213|AIH G-5]]; interference is a barrier and also a theory of forgetting [[25:212|AIH G-4]]. Answer the one the examiner asked about.

Overlap: FI.I.A covers motivation, anxiety, impatience, worry, fatigue, dehydration, apathy and the adult learner in more depth from the CFI ACS, and FOI.I.A covers perception and the laws of learning. Keep this Task's answers on its seven PTS items and use those lessons for depth.

Expect a learner quote and two questions: which mechanism, and what you will do. The AIH's answer to the second is to discuss the problem with common sense to restore motivation and self-confidence, with a professional counselor for severe cases [[25:45|AIH 2-12]]; for a possibly serious abnormality it is the unbiased evaluation flight [[25:49|AIH 2-16]].
gaps: The current AIH does not define 'control of human behavior'; this lesson maps the PTS item to related AIH content and says so.

No source gives a form or script for the pre-assessment; the AIH says only to verify the learner is physically and mentally ready [[25:39|AIH 2-6]]. Its IMSAFE checklist [[25:12|AIH 1-8]] is a reasonable start.

The AIH says to recommend a professional counselor in severe cases [[25:45|AIH 2-12]] but gives no referral process, and it does not say what to do if the unbiased instructor disagrees with you after the evaluation flight [[25:49|AIH 2-16]].
The AIH gives few instrument examples for defense mechanisms or barriers; the instrument examples in this lesson are illustrations and are marked as application.
AC 60-28, which the AIH names for English language questions [[25:98|AIH 4-5]], is not one of this course's build sources, so its current text is not taught here.

activities.title: True or false: what steers behavior
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: Threatening a learner with an unsatisfactory report is an effective way to change study habits.
cards.why: False. Learning is a psychological process, not necessarily a logical one; threats of unsatisfactory reports or reprisals may seem logical but are not effective psychologically [[25:59|AIH 3-8]].

cards.s: Negative motivation may be useful with the most overconfident and impulsive learners.
cards.why: True. Avoid it with all but those learners [[25:37|AIH 2-4]].

cards.s: Once a learner is motivated, motivation stays at a steady high level.
cards.why: False. Motivation does not remain at a uniformly high level; outside influences and inadequate instruction affect it [[25:37|AIH 2-4]].

cards.s: Once the immediate problem is solved, System 1 takes over again.
A learner who believes the instruction is inadequate still learns well if keen enough.
cards.why: False. Such learners do not learn well, and their motivation suffers no matter how intent they are on learning to fly [[25:43|AIH 2-10]].

cards.s: Behaviors that lead to satisfying outcomes are likely to be repeated.
cards.why: True. That is the law of effect, so create situations that promote success [[25:63|AIH 3-12]].

activities.title: Place the learner on the pyramid
activities.intro: Drag each instrument learner to the level of need it shows.

pins.label: Becomes the careful all-weather pilot she set out to be
Wants coworkers to respect him as an instrument pilot
Moved for the rating and knows no one at the school
Dreads the first unusual attitude recovery under the hood
Skipped lunch before a two-hour IFR lesson

activities.why: Levels from AIH Figure 2-3 and the text [[25:39|AIH 2-6]] [[25:40|AIH 2-7]]. External esteem relates to reputation, status, recognition and respect of associates [[25:40|AIH 2-7]]; security includes fear of certain flight regions [[25:39|AIH 2-6]].

activities.title: Name the defense mechanism
activities.intro: Tap a defense mechanism, then the learner behavior that shows it.

pairs.r: 'The examiner had it in for me; that is why I busted the approach'
'Nobody could study plates with my work hours,' said in full sincerity
Insists he never descended early, though the track log shows it
Scared of actual IMC, she brags that clouds never bother her
Talks about his future jet job instead of preparing for the next lesson
Angry at the check instructor, she is short with the dispatcher

activities.why: Definitions and the AIH's own examples on [[25:42|AIH 2-9]], [[25:43|AIH 2-10]] and [[25:44|AIH 2-11]].

activities.title: Confidence or challenge?
activities.intro: Tap a learner, then the approach the AIH points to.

items.t: Quiet learner who understands the procedure but is slow to act
Timid learner who shuts down after criticism
Learner discouraged after three tough approach lessons
Fast learner who shrugs off small errors
Learner who now flies the skill to standard every time
Motivated fast learner bored by drill on items already learned

activities.why: Build self-confidence, assign more easily attained goals and avoid too much criticism for quiet, timid or discouraged learners [[25:159|AIH 8-1]] [[25:160|AIH 8-2]]. Raise the standard for fast learners [[25:160|AIH 8-2]], present the next challenge once a skill meets the ACS or PTS standard [[25:38|AIH 2-5]], and advance a fast learner as soon as a goal is met [[25:45|AIH 2-12]].

activities.title: A possibly serious problem: the steps
activities.intro: Put the steps in order, first to last, then tap Check.
steps: Notice a possible abnormal reaction under stress
Evaluate it carefully, and check your own responses too
Arrange an evaluation flight with an instructor who does not know the learner
Confer with that instructor after the flight
If you both still suspect a serious deficiency, withhold endorsements and recommendations
activities.why: Signs of abnormal reactions call for careful evaluation, including of your own responses [[25:48|AIH 2-15]]; then the unbiased evaluation flight, the conference and, if warranted, withholding solo endorsements and practical test recommendations [[25:49|AIH 2-16]].

activities.title: Find the elements of communication
activities.intro: Drag each element to where it appears in Carol's ground lesson.
activities.why: Source, symbols and receiver [[25:95|AIH 4-2]]. The AIH names the model prop and desk lamp of Figure 4-1 as the symbols in this lesson [[25:95|AIH 4-2]] [[25:94|AIH 4-1]].

activities.title: Which barrier?
activities.intro: Tap a situation, then the barrier to effective communication it shows.

items.t: A learner who has never flown an approach nods at 'step-down fix'
'Time the magnetos' sends a new maintenance learner for a stopwatch
Calling an AMT a 'mechanic' calls up a picture of a car repair shop
'Take appropriate measures' on a bad approach instead of 'go around'
'Aircraft' makes one learner picture a helicopter and another an airship
'Fix it' when the learner drifts high on vectors to final
Engine noise in a trainer with no intercom
A learner who mistrusts you after a harsh debrief

activities.why: The four barriers and their examples [[25:97|AIH 4-4]] [[25:98|AIH 4-5]] [[25:99|AIH 4-6]]. Noise is an environmental factor and mistrust a psychological one [[25:99|AIH 4-6]].

activities.title: A partial panel lesson, one call at a time
activities.intro: You are the CFII for Omar, a private pilot with 210 hours halfway through his instrument rating. Make each call as his training unfolds.

steps.s: Omar arrives straight from a night shift, says he is 'fine' and wants to fly the partial panel lesson.
options: Fly as planned, since he says he is fine
Run a quick pre-assessment and change the plan if he is not ready
Fly, but do all of the flying yourself today
Send him home with a lecture on professionalism
steps.why: Verify the learner is physically and mentally ready with a pre-assessment [[25:39|AIH 2-6]]. Fatigue is the primary consideration in the length and frequency of flight lessons [[25:46|AIH 2-13]].

steps.s: Rested on the next try, he admits that partial panel makes him nervous.
options: Tell him there is nothing to worry about and move on
Surprise him with the failure so he learns to cope
Skip partial panel until he feels ready on his own
Treat the fear as normal and describe exactly what will happen
steps.why: Treat fears as a normal reaction rather than ignoring them, and introduce anxiety-causing maneuvers so learners know what to expect and what their reaction should be [[25:45|AIH 2-12]].

steps.s: With the attitude indicator covered, he fixates on the heading indicator and the altitude starts to drift.
options: Say 'Altimeter: 150 feet high, ease the nose down'
Say 'Watch your scan' and wait
Take the controls without a word
Explain cross-check theory in detail now
steps.why: Concrete, specific terms work better than abstractions [[25:99|AIH 4-6]]. Relying on a single instrument is poor technique, and holding altitude precisely needs the altimeter in the cross-check [[23:146|IFH 6-13]]. If you take the controls, use the positive exchange [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].

steps.s: ATC issues a reroute while he is still on partial panel. You want to explain why he fixated.
options: Explain now, while it is fresh in his mind
Talk him through it while ATC is still talking
Wait until he has copied and read back the clearance
Skip it; he will work it out on his own
steps.why: Adding even a simple activity reduces comprehension and recall of both tasks [[25:99|AIH 4-6]], and an instrument learner anticipating route changes can be too anxious to listen [[25:101|AIH 4-8]].

steps.s: In the debrief he says, 'That instrument failure was unrealistic; nobody could fly that.'
options: Tell him that is a classic defense mechanism
Agree, and drop partial panel work for now
Discuss the facts calmly to rebuild his motivation and confidence
Ignore it and move on to the next lesson
steps.why: Defense mechanisms are unconscious [[25:44|AIH 2-11]]; discuss the problem with common sense to restore motivation and self-confidence [[25:45|AIH 2-12]], and keep negative feedback private and nonjudgmental [[25:96|AIH 4-3]]. The PTS stresses partial panel skills because of fatal accidents involving failed primary flight instruments [[FAA-S-8081-9E:16|PTS Emphasis on Partial Panel Skills]].

steps.s: You want to confirm that he learned today's lesson.
options: Ask, 'Do you understand partial panel now?'
Ask, 'How will you cross-check when the attitude indicator fails?'
Tell him he did well and close the debrief
Ask him to read the IFH chapter at home
steps.why: Open-ended how and why questions bring full answers; closed-ended ones test only rote learning [[25:103|AIH 4-10]]. Then see on a later lesson whether the performance was retained [[25:100|AIH 4-7]].
